items.title: Big outages: one change pushed everywhere
items.text: 5 of 8 major outages pushed a global config or policy to every node fast. Another region on the same cloud would not stop it.

items.title: Regional failures are real, regions hold
items.text: Storms, voltage dips and fiber work each hit one region. The others kept running.

items.title: Retries and backlogs drag out recovery
items.text: AWS: DynamoDB was back in 2h 52m. The outage ran 14h 32m.

items.title: SLAs refund fees, not revenue
items.text: 99.99% allows 4.38 min a month. Credits cap at one month's fee, revenue is not covered.

notes: The answer first. We went through 13 cloud outages from June 2025 to September 2026, eight of them major, using what the vendors themselves published. Four findings. One: the outages with the widest blast radius were almost never hardware. A config or policy got pushed everywhere within seconds or minutes, and a second region in the same cloud does nothing against that. Two: single-region physical and network failures are real, from storms and power dips to fiber work and, in the Middle East, facilities destroyed outright. Multi-region does contain those. Three: recovery takes far longer than the fault itself, and what stretches it is retries, backlogs and everything restarting at once. Four: SLAs refund future fees. So our recommendation: take the second region to warm standby, not active-active. Give entry, identity and config rollout each a backup path that does not share a control plane. And ship throttling and backoff in Q4 without waiting for the new region.
